172.content: 1 tn Heb &quot;And he (the Lord) called (וַיִּקְרָא, vayyiqra&apos;) to Moses and the Lord spoke (וַיְדַבֵּר, vayÿdabber) to him from the tent of meeting.&quot; The MT assumes &quot;Lord&quot; in the first clause but places it in the second clause (after &quot;spoke&quot;). This is somewhat awkward, especially in terms of English style; most English versions reverse this and place &quot;Lord&quot; in the first clause (right after &quot;called&quot;). The Syriac version does the same. sn The best explanation for the MT of Lev 1:1 arises from its function as a transition from Exod 40 to Lev 1. The first clause, &quot;And he (the Lord) called to Moses,&quot; links v. 1 back to Exod 40:35, &quot;But Moses was not able to enter into the tent of meeting because the cloud had settled on it and the glory of the Lord had filled the tabernacle&quot; (cf. J. Milgrom, Leviticus [AB], 1:134). Exod 40:36-38 is a parenthetical explanation of the ongoing function of the cloud in leading the people through the wilderness. Since Moses could not enter the tent of meeting, the Lord &quot;called&quot; to him &quot;from&quot; the tent of meeting. 2 sn The second clause of v. 1, &quot;and the Lord spoke to him from the tent of meeting, saying,&quot; introduces the following discourse. This is a standard introductory formula (see, e.g., Exod 20:1; 25:1; 31:1; etc.). The combination of the first and second clauses is, therefore, &quot;bulky&quot; because of the way they happen to be juxtaposed in this transitional verse (J. E. Hartley, Leviticus [WBC], 8). The first clause of v. 1 connects the book back to the end of the Book of Exodus while the second looks forward the ritual legislation that follows in Lev 1:2ff. There are two &quot;Tents of Meeting&quot;: the one that stood outside the camp (see, e.g., Exod 33:7) and the one that stood in the midst of the camp (Exod 40:2; Num 2:2ff) and served as the Lord&apos;s residence until the construction of the temple in the days of Solomon (Exod 27:21; 29:4; 1 Kgs 8:4; 2 Chr 5:5, etc.; cf. 2 Sam 7:6). Exod 40:35 uses both &quot;tabernacle&quot; and &quot;tent of meeting&quot; to refer to the same tent: &quot;Moses could not enter the tent of meeting because the cloud had settled on it, and the glory of the Lord filled the tabernacle.&quot; It is clear that &quot;tent of meeting&quot; in Lev 1:1 refers to the &quot;tabernacle.&quot; The latter term refers to the tent as a &quot;residence,&quot; while the former refers to it as a divinely appointed place of &quot;meeting&quot; between God and man (see R. E. Averbeck, NIDOTTE 2:873-77 and 2:1130-34). This corresponds to the change in terms in Exod 40:35, where &quot;tent of meeting&quot; is used when referring to Moses&apos; inability to enter the tent, but &quot;tabernacle&quot; when referring to the Lord taking up residence there in the form of the glory cloud. The quotation introduced here extends from Lev 1:2 through 3:17, and encompasses the burnt, grain, and peace offering regulations. Compare the notes on Lev 4:1; 5:14; and 6:1 [5:20 HT] below.

3 tn &quot;When&quot; here translates the MT&apos;s כִּי (ki, &quot;if, when&quot;), which regularly introduces main clauses in legislative contexts (see, e.g., Lev 2:1, 4; 4:2, etc.) in contrast to אִם (&apos;im, &quot;if&quot;), which usually introduces subordinate sections (see, e.g., Lev 1:3, 10, 14; 2:5, 7, 14; 4:3, 13, etc.; cf. כִּי in Exod 21:2 and 7 as opposed to אִם in vv. 3, 4, 5, 8, 9, 10, and 11). sn Lev 1:1-2 serves as a heading for Lev 1-3 (i.e., the basic regulations regarding the presentation of the burnt, grain, and peace offerings) and, at the same time, leads directly into the section on &quot;burnt offerings&quot; in Lev 1:3. In turn, Lev 1:3-17 divides into three subsections, all introduced by אִם &quot;if&quot; (Lev 1:3-9, 10-13, and 14-17, respectively). Similar patterns are discernible throughout Lev 1:2-6:7 [5:26 HT]. 4 tn Heb &quot;a man, human being&quot; (אָדָם, &apos;adam), which in this case refers to any person among &quot;mankind,&quot; male or female, since women could also bring such offerings (see, e.g., Lev 12:6-8; 15:29-30; cf. HALOT 14 s.v. I אָדָם); cf. NIV &quot;any of you.&quot; 5 tn The verb &quot;presents&quot; is cognate to the noun &quot;offering&quot; in v. 2 and throughout the book of Leviticus (both from the root קרב [qrb]). One could translate the verb &quot;offers,&quot; but this becomes awkward and, in fact, inaccurate in some passages. For example, in Lev 9:9 this verb is used for the presenting or giving of the blood to Aaron so that he could offer it to the Lord. The blood is certainly not being &quot;offered&quot; as an offering to Aaron there. 6 tn The whole clause reads more literally, &quot;A human being (אָדָם, &apos;adam), if he brings from among you an offering to the Lord.&quot; 7 tn The shift to the second person plural verb here corresponds to the previous second person plural pronoun &quot;among you.&quot; It is distinct from the regular pattern of third person singular verbs throughout the rest of Lev 1-3. This too labels Lev 1:1-2 as an introduction to all of Lev 1-3, not just the burnt offering regulations in Lev 1 (J. Milgrom, Leviticus [AB], 1:146; cf. note 3 above). 8 tn Heb &quot;from the domesticated animal, from the herd, and from the flock.&quot; It is clear from the subsequent division between animals from the &quot;herd&quot; (בָּקָר, baqar, in Lev 1:3-9) and the &quot;flock&quot; (צֹאן, tso&apos;n; see Lev 1:10-13) that the term for &quot;domesticated animal&quot; (בְּהֵמָה, bÿhemah) is a general term meant to introduce the category of pastoral quadrupeds. The stronger disjunctive accent over בְּהֵמָה in the MT as well as the lack of a vav (ו) between it and בָּקָר also suggest בְּהֵמָה is an overall category that includes both &quot;herd&quot; and &quot;flock&quot; quadrupeds. sn The bird category (Lev 1:14-17) is not included in this introduction because bird offerings were, by and large, concessions to the poor (cf., e.g., Lev 5:7-10; 12:8; 14:21-32) and, therefore, not considered to be one of the primary categories of animal offerings.

9 sn The burnt offering (עֹלָה, &apos;olah) was basically a &quot;a gift of a soothing aroma to the Lord&quot; (vv. 9, 13, 17). It could serve as a votive or freewill offering (e.g., Lev 22:18-20), an accompaniment of prayer and supplication (e.g., 1 Sam 7:9-10), part of the regular daily, weekly, monthly, and festival cultic pattern (e.g., Num 28-29), or to make atonement either alone (e.g., Lev 1:4; 16:24) or in combination with the grain offering (e.g., Lev 14:20) or sin offering (e.g., Lev 5:7; 9:7). See R. E. Averbeck, NIDOTTE 4:996-1022. 10 tn Heb &quot;door&quot; (so KJV, ASV); NASB &quot;doorway&quot; (likewise throughout the book of Leviticus). The translation &quot;door&quot; or &quot;doorway&quot; may suggest a framed door in a casing to the modern reader, but here the term refers to the entrance to a tent. 11 tn The NIV correctly has &quot;it&quot; in the text, referring to the acceptance of the animal (cf., e.g., RSV, NEB, NLT), but &quot;he&quot; in the margin, referring to the acceptance of the offerer (cf. ASV, NASB, JB). The reference to a &quot;flawless male&quot; in the first half of this verse suggests that the issue here is the acceptability of the animal to make atonement on behalf of the offerer (Lev 1:4; cf. NRSV &quot;for acceptance in your behalf&quot;).

12 tn &quot;To make atonement&quot; is the standard translation of the Hebrew term כִּפֶּר, (kipper); cf. however TEV &quot;as a sacrifice to take away his sins&quot; (CEV similar). The English word derives from a combination of &quot;at&quot; plus Middle English &quot;one[ment],&quot; referring primarily to reconciliation or reparation that is made in order to accomplish reconciliation. The primary meaning of the Hebrew verb, however, is &quot;to wipe [something off (or on)]&quot; (see esp. the goal of the sin offering, Lev 4, &quot;to purge&quot; the tabernacle from impurities), but in some cases it refers metaphorically to &quot;wiping away&quot; anything that might stand in the way of good relations by bringing a gift (see, e.g., Gen 32:20 [21 HT], &quot;to appease; to pacify&quot; as an illustration of this). The translation &quot;make atonement&quot; has been retained here because, ultimately, the goal of either purging or appeasing was to maintain a proper relationship between the Lord (who dwelt in the tabernacle) and Israelites in whose midst the tabernacle was pitched (see R. E. Averbeck, NIDOTTE 2:689-710 for a full discussion of the Hebrew word meaning &quot;to make atonement&quot; and its theological significance).

13 tn Heb &quot;Then he&quot;; the referent (the offerer) has been specified in the translation for clarity. The LXX has &quot;they&quot; rather than &quot;he,&quot; suggesting that the priests, not the offerer, were to slaughter the bull (cf. the notes on vv. 6a and 9a). 14 tn Heb &quot;the son of the herd&quot;; cf. KJV &quot;bullock&quot;; NASB, NIV &quot;young bull.&quot; 15 tn &quot;Splash&quot; (cf. NAB) or &quot;dash&quot; (cf. NRSV) is better than &quot;sprinkle,&quot; which is the common English translation of this verb (זָרַק, zaraq; see, e.g., KJV, NASB, NIV, NLT). &quot;Sprinkle&quot; is not strong enough (contrast נָזָה [nazah], which does indeed mean &quot;to sprinkle&quot; or &quot;to splatter&quot;; cf. Lev 4:6).

16 tn Heb &quot;Then he&quot;; the referent (the offerer) has been specified in the translation for clarity. The LXX and Smr have &quot;they&quot; rather than &quot;he&quot; in both halves of this verse, suggesting that the priests, not the offerer, were to skin and cut the carcass of the bull into pieces (cf. the notes on vv. 5a and 9a).

17 tc A few medieval Hebrew mss, Smr, LXX, Syriac, and Tg. Onq. have plural &quot;priests&quot; here (cf. 1:5, 8) rather than the MT singular &quot;priest&quot; (cf. NAB). The singular &quot;priest&quot; would mean (1) Aaron, the (high) priest, or (2) the officiating priest, as in Lev 1:9 (cf. 6:10 [3 HT], etc.). &quot;The sons of Aaron&quot; is probably a textual corruption caused by conflation with Lev 1:5, 8 (cf. the remarks in J. E. Hartley, Leviticus [WBC], 13).

18 tc A few Hebrew mss, Smr, LXX, Syriac, and Tg. Onq. have the conjunction &quot;and&quot; before &quot;the head,&quot; which would suggest the rendering &quot;and the head and the suet&quot; rather than the rendering of the MT here, &quot;with the head and the suet.&quot; sn &quot;Suet&quot; is the specific term used for the hard, fatty tissues found around the kidneys of sheep and cattle. A number of modern English versions have simplified this to &quot;fat&quot; (e.g., NIV, NCV, TEV, CEV, NLT). 19 tn Heb &quot;on the wood, which is on the fire, which is on the altar.&quot; Cf. NIV &quot;on the burning wood&quot;; NLT &quot;on the wood fire.&quot;

20 tn Heb &quot;Finally, he&quot;; the referent (the offerer) has been specified in the translation for clarity. Once again, the MT assigns the preparation of the offering (here the entrails and legs) to the offerer because it did not bring him into direct contact with the altar, but reserves the actual placing of the sacrifice on the altar for the officiating priest (cf. the notes on vv. 5a and 6a). 21 tn Heb &quot;toward the altar,&quot; but the so-called locative ה (hey) attached to the word for &quot;altar&quot; can indicate the place where something is or happens (GKC 250 §90.d and GKC 373-74 §118.g; cf. also J. Milgrom, Leviticus [AB], 1:161). This is a standard way of expressing &quot;on/at the altar&quot; with the verb &quot;to offer up in smoke&quot; (Hiphil of קָטַר [qatar]; cf. also Exod 29:13, 18, 25; Lev 1:9, 13, 15, 17; 2:2, etc.). 22 tc A few Hebrew mss and possibly the Leningrad B19a ms itself (the basis of the BHS Hebrew text of the MT), under an apparent erasure, plus Smr, LXX, Syriac, and Tg. Ps.-J. suggest that Hebrew הוּא (hu&apos;, translated as &quot;it is&quot;) should be added here as in vv. 13 and 17. Whether or not the text should be changed, the meaning is the same as in vv. 13 and 17, so it has been included in the translation here. 23 sn The standard English translation of &quot;gift&quot; (אִשֶּׁה, &apos;isheh) is &quot;an offering [made] by fire&quot; (cf. KJV, ASV). It is based on a supposed etymological relationship to the Hebrew word for &quot;fire&quot; (אֵשׁ, &apos;esh) and is still maintained in many versions (e.g., NIV, RSV, NRSV, NLT; B. A. Levine, Leviticus [JPSTC], 7-8). For various reasons, including the fact that some offerings referred to by this term are not burned on the altar (see, e.g., Lev 24:9), it is probably better to understand the term to mean &quot;gift&quot; (J. E. Hartley, Leviticus [WBC], 22) or &quot;food gift&quot; (&quot;food offering&quot; in NEB and TEV; J. Milgrom, Leviticus [AB], 1:161-62). See R. E. Averbeck, NIDOTTE 1:540-49 for a complete discussion.

24 tn Heb &quot;And if from the flock is his offering, from the sheep or from the goats, for a burnt offering.&quot; Here &quot;flock&quot; specifies the broad category, with &quot;sheep or goats&quot; giving specific examples.
25 tn Heb &quot;Then he&quot;; the referent (the offerer) has been specified in the translation for clarity (so also in v. 13).

26 tn Heb &quot;from the [category] &apos;bird.&apos;&quot; 27 tn Heb &quot;from the sons of the pigeon,&quot; referring either to &quot;young pigeons&quot; (cf. KJV, NASB, NIV, NLT) or &quot;various species of pigeon&quot; (contrast J. Milgrom, Leviticus [AB], 1:168, with J. E. Hartley, Leviticus [WBC], 14).

28 tn The action here seems to involve both a twisting action, breaking the neck of the bird and severing its vertebrae, as well as pinching or nipping the skin to sever the head from the main body. Cf. NASB, NRSV &quot;wring off its head&quot;; NAB &quot;snap its head loose&quot;; NLT &quot;twist off its head.&quot; 29 tn Many English versions have &quot;it&quot; here, referring to the head of the bird, which the priest immediately tossed on the altar fire. However, &quot;it&quot; could be misunderstood to refer to the bird&apos;s body, so &quot;head&quot; is repeated in the present translation for clarity. As the following lines show, certain things needed to be done to the body of the bird before it could be placed on the altar.

30 tn Heb &quot;Then he&quot;; the referent (apparently still the priest) has been specified in the translation for clarity. 31 tn This translation (&quot;remove its entrails by [cutting off] its tail feathers&quot;) is based on the discussion in J. Milgrom, Leviticus (AB), 1:169-71, although he translates, &quot;remove its crissum by its feathers.&quot; Others possibilities include &quot;its crop with its contents&quot; (Tg. Onq., cf. NIV, NRSV; J. E. Hartley, Leviticus [WBC], 23) or &quot;its crop with its feathers&quot; (LXX, NASB, RSV; &quot;crop&quot; refers to the enlarged part of a bird&apos;s gullet that serves a pouch for the preliminary maceration of food). 32 tn The pronoun &quot;them&quot; here is feminine singular in Hebrew and refers collectively to the entrails and tail wing which have been removed.

33 tn Heb &quot;he shall not divide it.&quot; Several Hebrew mss, Smr, LXX, and Syriac have a vav on the negative, yielding the translation, &quot;but he shall not divide it into two parts.&quot; Cf. NIV &quot;not severing it completely&quot; (NRSV similar).

1 sn The &quot;grain offering&quot; ( מִנְחָה[minkhah]; here קָרְבַּן מִנְחָה, [qorbban minkhah], &quot;an offering of a grain offering&quot;) generally accompanied a burnt or peace offering to supplement the meat with bread (the libation provided the drink; cf. Num 15:1-10), thus completing the food &quot;gift&quot; to the Lord. It made atonement (see the note on Lev 1:4) along with the burnt offering (e.g., Lev 14:20) or alone as a sin offering for the poor (Lev 5:11-13). 2 tn The Hebrew term for &quot;choice wheat flour&quot; (סֹלֶת, selet) is often translated &quot;fine flour&quot; (cf. KJV, NAB, NIV, NCV), but it refers specifically to wheat as opposed to barley (B. A. Levine, Leviticus [JPSTC], 10). Moreover, the translation &quot;flour&quot; might be problematic, since the Hebrew term may designate the &quot;grits&quot; rather than the more finely ground &quot;flour&quot; (see J. Milgrom, Leviticus [AB], 1:179 as opposed to Levine, 10, and J. E. Hartley, Leviticus [WBC], 30). 3 sn This is not just any &quot;incense&quot; (קְטֹרֶת, qÿtoret; R. E. Averbeck, NIDOTTE 3:913-16), but specifically &quot;frankincense&quot; (לְבֹנָה, lÿvonah; R. E. Averbeck, NIDOTTE 2:756-57).

4 tn Heb &quot;and he&quot;; the referent has been specified in the translation for clarity. The syntax is strange here and might suggest that it was the offerer who scooped out a handful of the grain offering for the memorial portion (G. J. Wenham, Leviticus [NICOT], 66), but based on v. 9 below it should be understood that it was the priest who performed this act (see, e.g., NRSV &quot;After taking from it a handful of the choice flour and oil...the priest shall...&quot;; see also J. Milgrom, Leviticus [AB], 1:177, 181 and J. E. Hartley, Leviticus [WBC], 30). 5 sn The &quot;memorial portion&quot; (אַזְכָרָה, &apos;azkharah) was the part of the grain offering that was burnt on the altar (see the previous clause), as opposed to the remainder, which was normally consumed by the priests (v. 3; see the full regulations in Lev 6:14-23[7-16]). It was probably intended to call to mind (i.e., memorialize) before the Lord the reason for the presentation of the particular offering (see the remarks in R. E. Averbeck, NIDOTTE 1:335-39). 6 tn The words &quot;it is&quot; have been supplied. See the notes on Lev 1:9 and 2:3. There is no text critical problem here, but the syntax suggests the same translation.

7 tn Heb &quot;...is to Aaron and to his sons.&quot; The preposition &quot;to&quot; (לְ, lamed) indicates ownership. Cf. NAB, NASB, NIV and other English versions. 8 tn The words &quot;it is&quot; (הוּא, hu&apos;) are not in the MT, but are supplied for the sake of translation into English. The Syriac also for translational reasons adds it between &quot;most holy&quot; and &quot;from the gifts&quot; (cf. 1:13, 17). 9 tn Heb &quot;holy of holies&quot;; KJV, NASB &quot;a thing most holy.&quot;

1 sn The peace offering sacrifice primarily enacted and practiced communion between God and man (and between the people of God). This was illustrated by the fact that the fat parts of the animal were consumed on the altar of the Lord but the meat was consumed by the worshipers in a meal before God. This is the only kind of offering in which common worshipers partook of the meat of the animal. When there was a series of offerings that included a peace offering (see, e.g., Lev 9:8-21, sin offerings, burnt offerings, and afterward the peace offerings in vv. 18-21), the peace offering was always offered last because it expressed the fact that all was well between God and his worshiper(s). There were various kinds of peace offerings, depending on the worship intended on the specific occasion. The &quot;thank offering&quot; expressed thanksgiving (e.g., Lev 7:11-15; 22:29-30), the &quot;votive offering&quot; fulfilled a vow (e.g., Lev 7:16-18; 22:21-25), and the &quot;freewill offering&quot; was offered as an expression of devotion and praise to God (e.g., Lev 7:16-18; 22:21-25). The so-called &quot;ordination offering&quot; was also a kind of peace offering that was used to consecrate the priests at their ordination (e.g., Exod 29:19-34; Lev 7:37; 8:22-32). See R. E. Averbeck, NIDOTTE 1:1066-73 and 4:135-43. 2 tn Heb &quot;if a male if a female, perfect he shall present it before the Lord.&quot; The &quot;or&quot; in the present translation (and most other English versions) is not present in the Hebrew text here, but see v. 6 below.
3 tn See the remarks on Lev 1:3-5 above for some of the details of translation here.

4 tn Heb &quot;Then he&quot;; the referent (the person presenting the offering) has been specified in the translation for clarity (cf. the note on Lev 1:5). 5 tn Heb &quot;and all the fat on the entrails.&quot; The fat layer that covers the entrails as a whole (i.e., &quot;that covers the entrails&quot;) is different from the fat that surrounds and adheres to the various organs (&quot;on the entrails,&quot; i.e., surrounding them; J. Milgrom, Leviticus [AB], 1:205-7).

1 sn The quotation introduced here extends from Lev 4:2 through 5:13, and encompasses all the sin offering regulations. Compare the notes on Lev 1:1 above, and 5:14 and 6:1 [5:20 HT] below.

2 tn Heb &quot;And a person, when he sins in straying.&quot; The English translation of &quot;by straying&quot; (בִּשְׁגָגָה [bishgagah] literally, &quot;in going astray; in making an error&quot;) varies greatly, but almost all suggest that this term refers to sins that were committed by mistake or done not knowing that the particular act was sinful (J. Milgrom, Leviticus [AB], 1:228-29). See, e.g., LXX &quot;involuntarily&quot;; Tg. Onq. &quot;by neglect&quot;; KJV &quot;through ignorance&quot;; ASV, RSV, NJPS &quot;unwittingly&quot;; NASB, NIV, NRSV, NLT &quot;unintentionally&quot;; NAB, NEB &quot;inadvertently&quot;; NCV &quot;by accident.&quot; However, we know from Num 15:27-31 that committing a sin &quot;by straying&quot; is the opposite of committing a sin &quot;defiantly&quot; (i.e., בְּיַד רָמָה [bÿyad ramah] &quot;with a raised hand,&quot; v. 30). In the latter case the person, as it were, raises his fist in presumptuous defiance against the Lord. Thus, he &quot;blasphemes&quot; the Lord and has &quot;despised&quot; his word, for which he should be &quot;cut off from among his people&quot; (Num 15:30-31). One could not bring an offering for such a sin. The expression here in Lev 4:2 combines &quot;by straying&quot; with the preposition &quot;from&quot; which fits naturally with &quot;straying&quot; (i.e., &quot;straying from&quot; the Lord&apos;s commandments). For sins committed &quot;by straying&quot; from the commandments (Lev 4 throughout) or other types of transgressions (Lev 5:1-6) there was indeed forgiveness available through the sin offering. See R. E. Averbeck, NIDOTTE 2:94-95. 3 tn This is an emphatic use of the preposition מִן (min; see R. J. Williams, Hebrew Syntax, 56-57, §325). 4 tn The &quot;when&quot; clause (כִּי, ki) breaks off here before its resolution, thus creating an open-ended introduction to the following subsections, which are introduced by &quot;if&quot; (אִם [&apos;im] vv. 3, 13, 27, 32). Also, the last part of the verse reads literally, &quot;which must not be done and does from one from them.&quot;

5 tn Heb &quot;the anointed priest&quot; (so ASV, NAB, NASB, NIV, NRSV). This refers to the high priest (cf. TEV, CEV, NLT). 6 tn Heb &quot;to the guilt of the people&quot;; NRSV &quot;thus bringing guilt on the people.&quot; 7 tn Heb &quot;and he shall offer on his sin which he sinned, a bull, a son of the herd, flawless.&quot; 8 sn The word for &quot;sin offering&quot; (sometimes translated &quot;purification offering&quot;) is the same as the word for &quot;sin&quot; earlier in the verse. One can tell which rendering is intended only by the context. The primary purpose of the &quot;sin offering&quot; (חַטָּאת, khatta&apos;t) was to &quot;purge&quot; (כִּפֶּר, kipper, &quot;to make atonement,&quot; see 4:20, 26, 31, 35, and the notes on Lev 1:4 and esp. Lev 16:20, 33) the sanctuary or its furniture in order to cleanse it from any impurities and/or (re)consecrate it for holy purposes (see, e.g., Lev 8:15; 16:19). By making this atonement the impurities of the person or community were cleansed and the people became clean. See R. E. Averbeck, NIDOTTE 2:93-103.

1 tn Heb &quot;And a person when he sins.&quot; Most English versions translate this as the protasis of a conditional clause: &quot;if a person sins&quot; (NASB, NIV). sn The same expression occurs in Lev 4:2 where it introduces sins done &quot;by straying unintentionally from any of the commandments of the Lord which must not be done&quot; (see the notes there). Lev 5:1-13 is an additional section of sin offering regulations directed at violations other than those referred to by this expression in Lev 4:2 (see esp. 5:1-6), and expanding on the offering regulations for the common person in Lev 4:27-35 with concessions to the poor common person (5:7-13). 2 tn The words &quot;against one who fails to testify&quot; are not in the Hebrew text, but have been supplied to make sense of the remark about the &quot;curse&quot; (&quot;imprecation&quot; or &quot;oath&quot;; cf. ASV &quot;adjuration&quot;; NIV &quot;public charge&quot;) for the modern reader. For the interpretation of this verse reflected in the present translation see J. Milgrom, Leviticus (AB), 1:292-97. 3 tn The words &quot;what had happened&quot; are not in the Hebrew text, but are implied. 4 tn Heb &quot;and hears a voice of curse, and he is a witness or he saw or he knew, if he does not declare.&quot; 5 tn Heb &quot;and he shall bear his iniquity.&quot; The rendering &quot;bear the punishment (for the iniquity)&quot; reflects the use of the word &quot;iniquity&quot; to refer to the punishment for iniquity (cf. NRSV, NLT &quot;subject to punishment&quot;). It is sometimes referred to as the consequential use of the term (cf. Lev 5:17; 7:18; 10:17; etc.).

6 tc The insertion of the words &quot;when there is&quot; is a reflection of the few Hebrew mss, Smr, and LXX that have כִּי (ki, &quot;when, if&quot;; cf. vv. 3 and esp. 4) rather than the MT&apos;s אֲשֶׁר (&apos;asher, &quot;who&quot;). Many English versions render this as a conditional clause (&quot;if&quot;). 7 tn The word &quot;ceremonially&quot; has been supplied in the translation to clarify that the uncleanness involved is ritual or ceremonial in nature. 8 tn Heb &quot;and it is hidden from him,&quot; meaning that the person who contracted the ceremonial uncleanness was not aware at the time what had happened, but later found out that he had become ceremonially unclean. This same phrase occurs again in both vv. 3 and 4. 9 sn Lev 5:2-3 are parallel laws of uncleanness (contracted from animals and people, respectively), and both seem to assume that the contraction of uncleanness was originally unknown to the person (vv. 2 and 3) but became known to him or her at a later time (v. 3; i.e., &quot;has come to know&quot; in v. 3 is to be assumed for v. 2 as well). Uncleanness itself did not make a person &quot;guilty&quot; unless he or she failed to handle it according to the normal purification regulations (see, e.g., &quot;wash his clothes and bathe with water, and he will be unclean till evening,&quot; Lev 15:5 NIV; cf. Lev 11:39-40; 15:5-12, 16-24; Num 19, etc.). The problem here in Lev 5:2-3 is that, because the person had not been aware of his or her uncleanness, he or she had incurred guilt for not carrying out these regular procedures, and it would now be too late for that. Thus, the unclean person needs to bring a sin offering to atone for the contamination caused by his or her neglect of the purity regulations.
10 tn Heb &quot;or if he touches uncleanness of mankind to any of his uncleanness which he becomes unclean in it.&quot;

1 tn Although it has been used elsewhere in this translation as an English variation from the ubiquitous use of vav in Hebrew, in this instance &quot;then&quot; as a rendering for vav is intended to show that the Nadab and Abihu catastrophe took place on the inauguration day described in Lev 9. The tragic incident in Lev 10 happened in close temporal connection to the Lord&apos;s fire that consumed the offerings at the end of Lev 9. Thus, for example, the &quot;sin offering&quot; male goat referred to in Lev 10:16-19 is the very one referred to in Lev 9:15. 2 tn The expression &quot;strange fire&quot; (אֵשׁ זָרָה, &apos;esh zarah) seems imprecise (cf. NAB &quot;profane fire&quot;; NIV &quot;unauthorized fire&quot;; NRSV &quot;unholy fire&quot;; NLT &quot;a different kind of fire&quot;) and has been interpreted numerous ways (see the helpful summary in J. E. Hartley, Leviticus [WBC], 132-33). The infraction may have involved any of the following or a combination thereof: (1) using coals from someplace other than the burnt offering altar (i.e., &quot;unauthorized coals&quot; according to J. Milgrom, Leviticus [AB], 1:598; cf. Lev 16:12 and cf. &quot;unauthorized person&quot; אִישׁ זָר (&apos;ish zar) in Num 16:40 [17:5 HT], NASB &quot;layman&quot;), (2) using the wrong kind of incense (cf. the Exod 30:9 regulation against &quot;strange incense&quot; קְטֹרֶת זָרָה (qÿtoreh zarah) on the incense altar and the possible connection to Exod 30:34-38), (3) performing an incense offering at an unprescribed time (B. A. Levine, Leviticus [JPSTC], 59), or (4) entering the Holy of Holies at an inappropriate time (Lev 16:1-2).
3 tn See the note on 9:24a.

4 tn The Niphal verb of the Hebrew root קָדַשׁ (qadash) can mean either &quot;to be treated as holy&quot; (so here, e.g., BDB 873 s.v. קָּדַשׁ, LXX, NASB, and NEB) or &quot;to show oneself holy&quot; (so here, e.g., HALOT 1073 s.v. קדשׁnif.1, NIV, NRSV, NLT; J. Milgrom, Leviticus [AB], 1:595, 601-3; and J. E. Hartley, Leviticus [WBC], 133-34). The latter rendering seems more likely here since, in the immediate context, the Lord himself had indeed shown himself to be holy by the way he responded to the illegitimate incense offering of Nadab and Abihu. They had not treated the Lord as holy, so the Lord acted on his own behalf to show that he was indeed holy. 5 tn In this context the Niphal of the Hebrew root כָּבֵד (kaved) can mean &quot;to be honored&quot; (e.g., NASB and NIV here), &quot;be glorified&quot; (ASV, NRSV and NLT here), or &quot;glorify oneself, show one&apos;s glory&quot; (cf. NAB; e.g., specifically in this verse HALOT 455 s.v. כבדnif.3; J. Milgrom, Leviticus [AB], 1:595, 603-4; and J. E. Hartley, Leviticus [WBC], 126, 134). Comparing this clause with the previous one (see the note above), the point may be that when the Lord shows himself to be holy as he has done in 10:1-2, this results in him being honored (i.e., reverenced, feared, treated with respect) among the people. This suggests the passive rendering. It is possible, however, that one should use the reflexive rendering here as in the previous clause. If so, the passage means that the Lord showed both his holiness and his glory in one outbreak against Nadab and Abihu.

Similarly, שְׂאֵת also occurs in v. 19, and then v. 20 raises the issue of whether or not it appears to be &quot;lower (שָׁפָל, shafal) than the skin&quot; (cf. also 14:37 for a mark on the wall of a house), which may mean that the sore sinks below the surface of the skin rather than protruding above it as a swelling would (B. A. Levine, Leviticus [JPSTC], 76-77). Thus, one could translate here, for example, &quot;discoloration&quot; (so Milgrom and II שְׂאֵת &quot;spot, blemish on the skin&quot; in HALOT 1301 s.v. II שְׂאֵת) or &quot;local inflammation, boil, mole&quot; (so Levine). However, one could interpret &quot;lower&quot; as &quot;deeper,&quot; i.e., visibly extending below the surface of the skin into the deeper layers as suggested by J. E. Hartley, Leviticus (WBC), 188, 192. &quot;Swelling&quot; often extends deeply below the surface of the skin, it is certainly a common symptom of skin diseases, and the alternation of these two terms (i.e., &quot;deeper&quot; and &quot;lower&quot;) in vv. 25-26 below shows that they both refer to the same phenomenon (see also the note on v. 20 below), so it is retained in the present translation. 3 tn The etymology and meaning of this term is unknown. It could mean &quot;scab&quot; (KJV, ASV, NASB) or possibly &quot;rash&quot; (NIV, NLT), &quot;flaking skin,&quot; or an &quot;eruption&quot; (NRSV) of some sort. 4 tn Heb &quot;shiny spot&quot; or &quot;white spot,&quot; but to render this term &quot;white spot&quot; in this chapter would create redundancy in v. 4 where the regular term for &quot;white&quot; occurs alongside this word for &quot;bright spot.&quot; 5 tn Heb &quot;in the skin of his flesh&quot; as opposed to the head or the beard (v. 29). 6 tn Heb &quot;a mark [or stroke; or plague] of disease.&quot; In some places in this context (vv. 2, 3) it could be translated &quot;a contagious skin disease.&quot; Although the Hebrew term צָרָעַת (tsara&apos;at) rendered here &quot;diseased&quot; is translated in many English versions as &quot;leprosy,&quot; it does not refer to Hanson&apos;s disease, which is the modern technical understanding of the term &quot;leprosy&quot; (HALOT 1057 s.v. צָרְעַת a). There has been much discussion of the proper meaning of the term and the disease(s) to which it may refer (see, e.g., J. Milgrom, Leviticus [AB], 1:774-76, 816-26; J. E. Hartley, Leviticus [WBC], 187-89; and the literature cited by them). The further description of the actual condition in the text suggests that the regulations are concerned with any kind of infectious diseases that are observable on the surface of the skin and, in addition to that, penetrate below the surface of the skin (vv. 3-4) or spread further across the surface of the skin (vv. 5-8). It is true that, in the OT, the term &quot;disease&quot; is often associated specifically with white &quot;scaly&quot; skin diseases that resemble the wasting away of the skin after death (see Milgrom who, in fact, translates &quot;scale disease&quot;; cf., e.g., Exod 4:6-7 and Num 12:9-12, esp. v. 12), but here it appears to be a broader term for any skin disease that penetrates deep or spreads far on the body. Scaly skin diseases would be included in this category, but also other types. Thus, a &quot;swelling,&quot; &quot;scab,&quot; or &quot;bright spot&quot; on the skin might be a symptom of disease, but not necessarily so. In this sense, &quot;diseased&quot; is a technical term. The term &quot;infection&quot; can apply to any &quot;mark&quot; on the skin whether it belongs to the category of &quot;disease&quot; or not (compare and contrast v. 3, where the &quot;infection&quot; is not &quot;diseased,&quot; with v. 4, where the &quot;infection&quot; is found to be &quot;diseased&quot;). 7 tn Or &quot;it shall be reported to Aaron the priest.&quot; This alternative rendering may be better in light of the parallel use of the same expression in Lev 14:2, where the priest had to go outside the camp in order to inspect the person who had been diseased. Since the rendering &quot;he shall be brought to Aaron the priest&quot; might confuse matters there, this expression should be rendered &quot;it shall be reported&quot; both here in 13:2 (cf. also v. 9) and in 14:2. See, however, the further note on 14:2 below, where it is argued that the diseased person would still need to &quot;be brought&quot; to the priest even if this happened outside the camp. Most English versions retain the idea of the afflicted person being &quot;brought&quot; to the priest for inspection.

8 tn Heb &quot;and the priest shall see the infection.&quot; 9 tn There is no &quot;if&quot; expressed, but the contrast between the priestly finding in this verse and the next verse clearly implies it. 10 tn Heb &quot;and the appearance of the infection is deep &apos;from&apos; (comparative מִן, min, &quot;deeper than&quot;) the skin of the his flesh.&quot; See the note on v. 20 below. 11 tn For the translation &quot;diseased infection&quot; see the note on v. 2 above. Cf. TEV &quot;a dreaded skin disease&quot;; NIV &quot;an infectious skin disease&quot;; NLT &quot;a contagious skin disease.&quot; 12 tn The pronoun &quot;it&quot; here refers to the &quot;infection,&quot; not the person who has the infection (cf. the object of &quot;examine&quot; at the beginning of the verse). 13 tn Heb &quot;he shall make him unclean.&quot; The verb is the Piel of טָמֵא (tame&apos;) &quot;to be unclean.&quot; Here it is a so-called &quot;declarative&quot; Piel (i.e., &quot;to declare unclean&quot;), but it also implies that the person is put into the category of actually being &quot;unclean&quot; by the pronouncement itself (J. E. Hartley, Leviticus [WBC], 175; cf. the corresponding opposite in v. 6 below).

Since he or she had been declared &quot;unclean&quot; by a priest (Lev 13:3) and was, therefore, required to remain outside the camp (13:46), the formerly diseased person could not reenter the camp until he or she had been declared &quot;clean&quot; by a priest (cf. Lev 13:6 for &quot;declaring clean.&quot;). See especially J. Milgrom, Leviticus (AB), 1:831, who supports this rendering both here and in Lev 13:2 and 9. B. A. Levine, however, prefers the rendering in the text (Leviticus [JPSTC], 76 and 85). It is the most natural meaning of the verb (i.e., &quot;to be brought&quot; from בּוֹא [bo&apos;, &quot;to come&quot;] in the Hophal stem, which means &quot;to be brought&quot; in all other occurrences in Leviticus other than 13:2, 9, and 14:2; see only 6:30; 10:18; 11:32; and 16:27), it suits the context well in 13:2, and the rendering &quot;to be brought&quot; is supported by 13:7b, &quot;he shall show himself to the priest a second time.&quot; Although it is true that the priest needed to go outside the camp to examine such a person, the person still needed to &quot;be brought&quot; to the priest there. 1 tn Heb &quot;Man man.&quot; The reduplication is a way of saying &quot;any man&quot; (cf. Lev 17:3; 22:18, etc.; see the distributive repetition of the noun in GKC 395-96 §123.c). 2 tn The term &quot;discharge&quot; actually means &quot;to flow,&quot; whether referring to a full flow as at a spring of water (Ps 78:20 and parallels) or in reference to the promised land as &quot;a land flowing with milk and honey&quot; (Exod 3:8 and parallels). 3 tn Heb &quot;man, man when there is a discharge from his flesh.&quot; The repetition of the word &quot;man&quot; is distributive, meaning &quot;any [or &quot;every&quot;] man&quot; (GKC 395-96 §123.c). It is well-recognized that the term &quot;flesh&quot; (i.e., &quot;body&quot;) in this chapter refers regularly and euphemistically to the male and female genital members or areas of the body (HALOT 164 s.v. בָּשָׂר 5.b; see also, e.g., B. A. Levine, Leviticus [JPSTC], 93). The euphemism has been retained in this translation since it is, in fact, intended in the Hebrew text. Some English versions partially remove the euphemism (e.g., NAB &quot;from his private parts&quot;; NRSV &quot;from his member&quot;) while some remove it completely (e.g., NLT &quot;a genital discharge&quot;; TEV &quot;from his penis&quot;; CEV &quot;with an infected penis&quot;).

4 tn The LXX has &quot;this the law of his uncleanness...&quot; (cf. v. 32 and compare, e.g., 13:59; 14:2, 56). 5 tc Smr, LXX, and the Paleo-Hebrew Leviticus Scroll from Qumran (11QpaleoLev; Fragment G contains Lev 14:52-15:5 and 16:2-4, and agrees with the LXX of Lev 15:3b) are in essential (although not complete) agreement against the MT in Lev 15:3b and are to be preferred in this case. The shorter MT text has probably arisen due to a lengthy haplography. See K. A. Mathews, &quot;The Leviticus Scroll (11QpaleoLev) and the Text of the Hebrew Bible,&quot; CBQ 48 (1986): 177-78, 198; D. N. Freedman, &quot;Variant Readings in the Leviticus Scroll from Qumran Cave 11,&quot; CBQ 36 (1974): 528-29; D. N. Freedman and K. A. Mathews, The Paleo-Hebrew Leviticus Scroll, 32. The MT of Lev 15:3 reads: &quot;Now this is his uncleanness in [regard to] his discharge - whether his body secretes his discharge or blocks his discharge, this is his uncleanness.&quot; Smr adds after MT&apos;s &quot;blocks his discharge&quot; the following: &quot;he is unclean; all the days that his body has a discharge or his body blocks his discharge, this is his uncleanness.&quot; Thus, the MT appears to skip from Smr טמא הוא &quot;he is unclean&quot; in the middle of the verse to יא/טמאתו הו &quot;this is his uncleanness&quot; at the end of the verse, leaving out &quot;he is unclean; all the days that his body has a discharge or his body blocks his discharge&quot; (cf. the BHS footnote). 11Q1 (paleoLeva frag. G) is indeed fragmentary, but it does have ימי ז בו כל &quot;...in him, all the days of the fl[ow],&quot; supporting Smr and LXX tradition. The LXX adds after MT &quot;blocks his discharge&quot; the following: &quot;all the days of the flow of his body, by which his body is affected by the flow,&quot; followed by &quot;it is his uncleanness&quot; (i.e., the last two words of the MT). sn The contrast between the dripping or flowing from the male sexual member as opposed to there being a blockage is important. One might not understand that even though a blockage actually causes a lack of discharge, it is still unclean. 6 tn Heb &quot;it is his uncleanness,&quot; but the last clause recapitulates the effect of the first clause in this verse, both of which introduce the regulations for such uncleanness in the following verses. In other words, whether his discharge flows from his penis or is blocked in it, he is still unclean and must proceed according to the following regulations (vv. 4ff).

2 tn Heb &quot;into the holy place from house to the veil-canopy.&quot; In this instance, the Hebrew term &quot;the holy place&quot; refers to &quot;the most holy place&quot; (lit. &quot;holy of holies&quot;), since it is the area &quot;inside the veil-canopy&quot; (cf. Exod 26:33-34). The Hebrew term פָּרֹכֶת (parokhet) is usually translated &quot;veil&quot; or &quot;curtain,&quot; but it seems to have stretched not only in front of but also over the top of the ark of the covenant which stood behind and under it inside the most holy place, and thus formed more of a canopy than simply a curtain (see R. E. Averbeck, NIDOTTE 3:687-89). 3 tn Heb &quot;to the faces of the atonement plate.&quot; The exact meaning of the Hebrew term כַּפֹּרֶת (kapporet) here rendered &quot;atonement plate&quot; is much debated. The traditional &quot;mercy seat&quot; (KJV, ASV, NASB, NRSV) does not suit the cognate relationship between this term and the Piel verb כִּפֶּר (kipper, &quot;to make atonement, to make expiation&quot;). The translation of the word should also reflect the fact that the most important atonement procedures on the Day of Atonement were performed in relation to it. Since the Lord would &quot;appear in the cloud over the atonement plate,&quot; and since it was so closely associated with the ark of the covenant (the ark being his &quot;footstool&quot;; cf. 1 Chr 28:2 and Ps 132:7-8), one could take it to be the place of his throne at which he accepts atonement. See J. Milgrom, Leviticus (AB), 1:1014; J. E. Hartley, Leviticus (WBC), 234-35; and R. E. Averbeck, NIDOTTE 2:691, 699. Cf. NIV &quot;the atonement cover&quot;; NCV &quot;the lid on the Ark&quot;; NLT &quot;the Ark&apos;s cover - the place of atonement.&quot;

1 tn Cf. the note on Lev 22:21. Some take this as an expression for fulfilling a vow, &quot;to fulfill a vow&quot; (e.g., HALOT 927-28 s.v. פלא piel and NASB; cf. NRSV &quot;in fulfillment of a vow&quot;) or, alternatively, &quot;to make a vow&quot; or &quot;for making a vow&quot; (HALOT 928 s.v. פלא piel [II פלא]). Perhaps it refers to the making a special vow, from the verb פָלָא (pala&apos;, &quot;to be wonderful; to be remarkable&quot;), cf. Milgrom, Numbers [JPSTC], 44. B. A. Levine, Leviticus (JPSTC), 151 and 193, suggests that this is a special term for &quot;setting aside a votive offering&quot; (related to פָלָה, palah, &quot;to set aside&quot;). In general, the point of the expression seems to be that this sacrifice is a special gift to God that arose out of special circumstances in the life of the worshiper. 2 tn Heb &quot;in your valuation, persons to the Lord,&quot; but &quot;in your valuation&quot; is a frozen form and, therefore, the person (&quot;your&quot;) does not figure into the translation (see J. E. Hartley, Leviticus [WBC], 73). Instead of offering a person to the Lord one could redeem that person with the appropriate amount of money delineated in the following verses (see the note on Lev 5:15 above and the explanation in Hartley, 480-81).
3 tn Heb &quot;your conversion value shall be [for] the male.&quot; 4 tn Heb &quot;from a son of twenty years and until a son of sixty years.&quot; 5 tn See the note on Lev 5:15.

195.content: &lt;Praefatio&gt;Hebraice VAIICRA ISICHIUS in Levit. Liber iste Leviticus dicitur quia scilicet in hoc nomine totius libri argumentum manifestatur. Tribus Levi tabernaculi ministerium sortita est, in quo sacrificia, et primitias, et primogenitorum oblationes offerri praeceptum est, quia omnia sacrificia ad Levitas pertinent Num. 18.. A quibus liber iste congruum sortitus est nomen, qui haec omnia digerit per ordinem. Latine &lt;Offertorius&gt;vel &lt;sacrificativus&gt;dicitur, quia de sacrificiis et caeremoniis agit. Hic bene post Exodum ponitur: in eo enim tabernaculum ordinatur, in hoc ea continentur quae Dominus Moysi de tabernaculo loquebatur, et tabernaculi caeremoniae. Si quis autem quaerat quare libri legis divisi sunt, cum historia tempore indivisa sit, respondendum est: ut fastidium scilicet lectori auferret librorum divisio, sicut et viae spatia dividit viator, ut tanquam divisus minuatur labor. Rabanus ab Isichio Hierosolymorum episcopo, qui Leviticum satis plene exposuit, multa collegit, et ab aliis quoque Patribus, qui ejus aliquas sententias exposuerunt, quaedam operi suo apposuit, et ex confuso sententiarum ordine quemdam expositionis ordinem multorum doctorum sententias alternando composuit. ISICHIUS in Levit. Prae omnibus necesse est interpretationem legis ad anagogen trahi, et spiritualem intelligentiam in littera prescrutari. Hoc enim non contradicit legi, sed eam defendit. Spiritualem quippe intellectum diligenter esse inquirendum etiam ipse Christus ostendit, qui in parabolis suis Matth. 13. agrum, mundum; agricolam seminantem semen bonum, justos; zizania, malignos; messores quoque, angelos; et inimicum superseminantem, diabolum appellavit. Quis ergo vetat bovem eum qui operatur justitiam, appellare; sicut ovem, simplicem; et innocentem, columbam: et turturem sublimius agentes et contemplationi vacantes? Nunquid non Ezechiel Hierusalem leaenam dixit: et catulum ejus, Eliachim, qui ductus est in Aegyptum, et alium catulum Joachim in Babylonem ductum? Ezech. 19. Non solum quae in parabolis dicta sunt, sed et quae secundum historiam sunt, ad sublimiorem ducenda esse intellectum Paulus ostendit, dicens: &lt;Scriptum est quoniam Abraham habuit duos filios,&gt;etc.; post quae addidit: &lt;Quae sunt secundum allegoriam dicta: haec enim sunt duo Testamenta,&gt;etc. Gal. 4.. Fortassis autem noxia erit littera spoliata spirituali intelligentia, et variis reprehensionibus obnoxia. Unde per Ezechielem et bonam legem, et non bonam Dominus appellat, dicens: &lt;Dedi eis praecepta mea, et judicia mea ostendi eis, quae faciat homo et vivat in eis.&gt;Et alibi: &lt;Dedi eis mandata non bona, et judicia in quibus non vivant.&gt;Patet ergo bona esse et non bona; et in quibus vivant et in quibus non vivant: qui enim custodit sanctum Spiritum, vivit in eis; qui autem secundum carnem, moritur, quia vitam non cognoscit in eis. Deinde legislator non semper, sed certo tempore voluit custodiri legis superficiem, ut reprimeret duram Judaeorum cervicem; unde: &lt;Scio quod populus iste durae cervicis sit&gt;Exod. 32.; Osee autem vocat Judaeos vitulam consternantem, quae scilicet nullo modo domatur. Et alibi: &lt;Ephraim vitula docta diligere trituram, transivi super pulchritudinem colli ejus&gt;Osee. 10.; in quo obedientia significatur. Jugum enim legis imposuit, ut humiliati libenter susciperent leve et suave jugum Evangelii Matth. 12.. ORIG., homil. 1, in Levit. Si secundum quosdam etiam nostrorum simplicem intellectum sequamur, et absque ulla, ut ipsi nos ridere solent, stropha verbi et allegoriae nubilo vocem legislatoris excipiamus, ego ecclesiasticus sub fide Christi vivens, et in medio Ecclesiae positus, ad sacrificandum vitulos vel agnos, et ad offerendam similam cum thure et oleo, divini praecepti auctoritate compellor: ipse ergo Dominus, ipse Spiritus sanctus deprecandus est, ut omnem nebulam peccati quae visum cordis nostri obscurat, auferre dignetur, ut spiritualem intelligentiam intueamur, secundum illud: &lt;Revela oculos meos et considerabo mirabilia,&gt;etc. Psal. 118.. ISID. Omnis hostiarum diversitas Christi hostiam praefigurabat. Unde, &lt;veritate oblata, cessavit umbra&gt;I Cor. 15., verum sacrificium veri et aeterni sacerdotis praefigurans. Ideo autem hostiis animalium propter emundationem oblatis, una vera hostia Christi promittebatur, in qua fieret remissio peccatorum contractorum de carne et sanguine, qui regnum Dei non possidebunt: quia substantia corporalis in coelestem mutabitur qualitatem. Christus in vitulo propter virtutem crucis offerebatur; in agno, propter innocentiam; in ariete, propter principatum; in hirco, propter similitudinem carnis peccati; in turture et columba, quia Deus et homo. Mediator enim Dei et hominum in duarum substantiarum conjunctione monstrabatur; in similaginis conspersione, credentium per aquam baptismi collectam esse Ecclesiam, id est corpus Christi, ostendebatur. Nos autem moraliter offerimus vitulum, cum carnis superbiam vincimus; agnum, cum irrationabiles motus corrigimus; haedum, cum lasciviam superamus; columbam, dum simplices sumus; turturem, dum casti sumus, vel dum castitatem servamus; panes azymos, cum non in fermento malitiae, sed in azymis sinceritatis et veritatis epulamur. RAB. Singula sacrificia, imo singulas pene syllabas, et vestes Aaron, et totum Leviticum ordinem coelestia dicit spirare sacramenta. Origenes quoque ait: Quia sicut in novissimis diebus Verbum Dei ex Maria virgine carne vestitum processit in mundum; cujus caro ab omnibus videbatur, divinitas paucis et electis cognita tegebatur: sic verbum Dei per prophetas profertur ad homines, ibi carnis, hic litterae velamine tectum. Littera tanquam caro aspicitur: spiritualis sensus tanquam divinitas sentitur. &lt;Vocavit,&gt;etc. ISICH. in Levit. Per conjunctionem sequentia jungit praecedentibus; initium, scilicet libri hujus cum fine praecedentis: unius enim et ejusdem diei opus in utroque continetur. Liber quoque Numeri, quia nihil habet medium inter se et Leviticum, simile sortitur prooemium; hoc est: &lt;Locutusque est Dominus ad Moysen in deserto Sinai,&gt;etc. Num. 1.. Nihil ergo post historiam Levitici ante historiam Numeri populus egit: neque enim locum mutaverat, quia necdum tabernaculum dedicaverat, nec multum temporis praeterierat. In primo quippe mense secundi anni, ejusdem mensis initio agere coeperunt. In Exodo autem et Genesi, quia multum temporis medium, mortis Joseph et egressionis filiorum Israel, fluxerat, conjunctio non obtinet principium, sed opportunum dispensationi eorum dispensatur exordium: &lt;Haec sunt nomina filiorum Israel, qui ingressi sunt Aegyptum.&gt;ISICH. Secundum 70. &lt;Revocavit.&gt;Sicut secundum eos &lt;revocavit&gt;Deus Beseleel ex nomine, quando praecepit fieri tabernaculum secundum figuram, quae ostensa est in monte: ergo et nunc quamdam sacrificiorum intelligibilium imaginem describere praecepit; haec revocatio quippe quamdam dispensationem rerum vel verborum ad superiora respicientium innuit. ORIG. hom. 1 in Levit. &lt;Vocavit autem,&gt;etc. In principio, etc., usque ad qui ad haec audienda interiores aures afferunt mundas. ISICH. in Levit. Quod non diligat Deus Judaeorum sacrificia, etc., usque ad et aperte haec vocatio dispensationem verborum vel rerum respicientium ad superiora innuit. ORIG. homil. 1 Exod. Hominem quem primo posuit ad offerendum Domino, etc., usque ad sacrificium quoque duplex est quod et terrestria et coelestia salvet. ID., ibid. Homo qui ad imaginem Dei et similitudinem factus rationabiliter vivit, etc., usque ad et collum ejus sicut turturis. ISICH. in Levit. Simplicem designat hominem, etc., usque ad jumentis etiam salus conceditur. ID. Sacrificium Deus exigit ut nobis proficiat, non sibi, etc., usque ad quae tandem pro nobis aut contra nos testimonium dicant.

&lt;De armento,&gt;etc. ISID. Primum sacrificium est vitulus, id est Christus, &lt;de armento,&gt;id est de patriarcharum stirpe progenitus, qui aratro suae crucis terram carnis nostrae perdomuit, et Spiritus sancti semen virtutum fruge ditavit. ORIG., ut supra. Vitulus superbus, caro nostra, etc., usque ad oleum autem charitatis et pacis et aliarum virtutum non habuerunt. &lt;Ad placandum,&gt;etc. Juxta LXX autem hoc acceptum dicit offerenti, scilicet si enim acceptum nobis vere sit, et cor nostrum recte judicans, nullique adhaerens passioni, munus ad suscipiendum dignum probaverit: tunc orare in conspectu Domini, id est remissionem possumus obtinere. Unde coram ipso suadebimus corda nostra, quia si reprehenderit nos cor nostrum, scimus quia major est Deus corde nostro, et cognoscit omnia, etc.

&lt;Ponetque,&gt;etc. Quod nos hostiam dicimus, Graece dicitur, in quo intelligibile holocaustum significatur. Spiritualiter enim fructificat, qui per spiritualem conversationem efficitur holocaustum: propter quod qui offert, manum in caput hostiae ponit, quod significat initium praedictae conversationis, quam qui offert, ipse sibi causa promissionis est. Sponte enim offert, quia donum est, et omne donum voluntarium est. Si enim promissionem suam trangressus fuerit, seipsum accusat, cum poenas luerit. Sic autem acceptabilis erit, et ad expiationem suam proficiens, cum positione manus manifestaverit, quia sponte non necessitate obtulerit.

&lt;Immolabitque,&gt;etc. ISICH. in Levit. Non solum enim propriam conscientiam et conversationem Deo debemus offerre, etc., usque ad sicut Christus ostium appellatur, sic doctrina apostolica quam largitur. &lt;Filii Aaron.&gt;ORIG., ubi supra. De genere Aaron erant Anna et Caiphas, et alii qui Christum pronuntiaverunt esse reum mortis, et effuderunt sanguinem ejus ad basim altaris: ibi enim est occisus, ubi altare erat et basis ejus, unde: &lt;Non capit prophetam perire extra Hierusalem.&gt;

&lt;Detractaque,&gt;etc. ORIG., ibid. Sacerdos pellem detrahit, etc., usque ad terrena coelestibus et divinis humana sociavit. ID Intestina cum pedibus jubet aqua dilui, in significationem baptismi. Intestina lavat, qui conscientiam purgat; pedes abluit, qui consummationem suscipit sacramenti. &lt;Qui enim mundus est, non indiget nisi ut pedes lavet, sed est mundus totus&gt;Joan. 15.: nec quisquam potest habere partem cum Jesu, nisi laverit pedes ejus. ISICH. in Levit. Pellis detrahitur cum divitiis et quibuscunque saecularibus exspoliamur, etc., usque ad Christum imitantes sicut possumus. GREG. lib. I Moral., cap. 40. Pellem hostiae detrahimus, etc., usque ad nihil lubricum in ara suae orationis imponat.

&lt;Quod si,&gt;etc. ISICH. in Levit. Paucis immutatis eadem dicit, etc., usque ad unde: Filius non portabit iniquitatem patris, etc. &lt;Anniculum,&gt;etc. ISID. Agnus oblatus, Christus innocens crucifixus. Unde: &lt;Ecce agnus Dei, ecce qui tollit peccata mundi.&gt;Bene haedus offertur, quia per mortem Christi jugulatur diabolus auctor peccati. ISICH. Hoc de bobus non praecepit, etc., usque ad propterea holocaustum dicitur etiam sine operatione justitiae.

&lt;Ad latus,&gt;id est Gentilitatem altare respicit, quia pro gentibus celebrata est passio Christi. Nos vero ad aquilonarem partem altaris sacrificium offerimus, dum memoriter passionem Christi pro gentibus factam credimus.

&lt;Omnia adolebit.&gt;Haec omnia super altare offerentem ponere jubet ut omnem nostrum hominem, spiritualibus scripturis quae de intelligibili altari Dominici corporis dictae sunt, coaptemus, et ad imitationem ejus vivere studeamus. &lt;Et odorem.&gt;Quando sacrificium nostrum holocaustum fit, et offerimus omnia super intelligibile altare, tanquam imitatores Christi conversationem vitae nostrae conformantes ei, tunc offertur Domino odor suavissimus.

&lt;Si autem.&gt;ISID. Turtur, caro Christi, secundum illud Salomonis: &lt;Pulchrae sunt genae tuae sicut turturis:&gt;Columba Spiritum sanctum significat. Unde: &lt;Super quem videris Spiritum descendentem sicut columbam, hic est Filius meus.&gt;Turtur ergo columba caro Christi est Spiritui sociata: haec tria sacrificia offert homo, id est Christus, de bobus scilicet, pecoribus, et avibus. ISICH. &lt;in Levit.&gt;Admirabilis verborum subtilitas, etc., &lt;usque ad,&gt;contemplantur et sapiunt coelestia, ubi Christus est in dextera Dei sedens.

&lt;Anima,&gt;etc. A meliori parte totum hominem significat: requirit enim spiritualem et perfectum auditorem, quia anima est sapientiae capax, non caro. ISID. &lt;Anima,&gt;etc. Quartum sacrificium offert anima. Simila Ecclesiam significat, quae de multis personis quasi granis est collecta, legis et Evangelii mola inter litteram et spiritum separata, per aquam baptismi adunata, chrismate peruncta et solidata spirituali igne; per humilitatem fit accepta hostia. ORIG. &lt;hom 2 in Lev. Anima.&gt;Quae scilicet nec vitulum habet, etc.; usque ad oleo divinae misericordiae vel gratiae. Mystice, significat, sicut ibi: &lt;Cunctae animae quae ingessae sunt cum Jacob in Aegyptum,&gt;etc. Gen. 46. Lucas autem ait: &lt;Eramus autem omnes animae in navi ducentae septuaginta sex&gt;Act. 27.. Forsitan per animam, Gentilem significat. Supra enim filiis Israel praecepit, ut sacrificia offerrent cum sanguine. Hic autem qui est sine lege, offerre praecipiens, non dicit homo, sicut supra, sed &lt;anima.&gt;Animalis erat Gentilis, non intelligens ea quae sunt Dei, sed vocatur ad oblationem misericordia Dei, ut percipiat salutem; cum pro peccatis sacrificia disponit, qui nec habet ovem nec capram, turturem vel columbam offerre praecipitur; qui nec habet illud, similam. Non enim jam ex operibus, ut pauper virtutibus, sed sola cognitione Dei salvatur, quae licet principium sit salutis, tamen thus et oleum, supponendum, ut gratia de eleemosynis et orationibus misceatur. Unde angelus ad Cornelium ait: &lt;Orationes tuae et eleemosynae tuae ascenderunt ad Dominum&gt;Act. 10.. In thure interiores curantur passiones, et fumo ejus sanantur occuli ex infirmitate lacrymantes. Oratio quippe animae passiones sanat, oculos interiores curat ab ignorantia lacrymas ex aegritudine peccati accendentes fugat. &lt;Filios,&gt;ministros Ecclesiae; quia quidquid offerimus, cum sanctis Ecclesiae doctoribus conferre debemus. Unde Paulus cum apostolis contulit Evangelium, ne in vacuum cucurrisset Gal. 2.. &lt;Quorum.&gt;Unitas Ecclesiae pugillum similae tollit, quia pro capacitate sensus unusquisque fidelis Scripturae scientiam debet appetere. Unde: &lt;Non plus sapere quam oportet, sed sapere ad sobrietatem. Quorum unus,&gt;etc. Rom. 12.. Notandum quod pugillus similae et olei, totum vero thus offerri jubetur; quia sapientia quae in simila, et charitas vel misericordia quae in oleo signatur, in hac vita non possunt esse plena. Unde: &lt;Videmus nunc per speculum in aenigmate:&gt;et, &lt;nunc cognosco ex parte,&gt;etc. I Cor. 12.. Olei quoque pars offertur, quia misericordia nunquam impletur, quia etsi miserearis quantum potes, plus tamen debes velle. Charitas etiam quae oleo figuratur, in praesenti inchoatur, in futuro perficietur. Thus autem totum crematur, quia semper orationi insistitur. &lt;Similae.&gt;Scientiae vel cognitionis Dei. Accepta enim est scientia a Deo, quam fides comprehendere potest, et sicut qui pugillo vult plus comprehendere, nihil proficit, totum quippe decurrit: sic fides est mensura scientiae Dei. &lt;Credere enim oportet accedentem ad Deum, et quod non est ex fide, peccatum est&gt;Heb. 11.. &lt;Memoriale,&gt;etc., cognitionis Dei perfectam scientiam, cujus memores erimus, quae nunquam destruitur; et eam quae nunc est, non ut contrariam, destruit, sed partem minimam esse per plenitudinem suam ostendit: &lt;Cum enim venerit quod perfectum est, evacuabitur quod ex parte est&gt;I Cor. 13..

&lt;De sacrificio,&gt;etc. ISICH. in Lev. De illa scilicet perfecta et in coelis abscondita, in Christoque reposita scientia, &lt;in quo sunt omnes thesauri sapientiae et scientiae absconditi&gt;Col. 2.. &lt;Aaron,&gt;montanus interpretatur, id est, altiora de Deo intelligens; vel arcanus, quasi in se legem Dei et eloquia habens: hic sacrificium offerre potest. Sanctum sanctorum, est de oblationibus Domino: partile enim est quod reliquum est, omnes tamen scientias superans et ad perfectionem exaltans

&lt;Cum obtuleris sacrificium,&gt;etc. ISICH., ibid. Sacrificium Christus pro nobis immolatus. &lt;Coctum in clibano&gt;virginis, scilicet utero. Clibanus enim panem suscipit et ignem: sic uterus virginis panem vitae, id est, Dei verbum, et ignem Spiritus sancti de coelo suscepit. Unde: &lt;Spiritus sanctus superveniet in te,&gt;etc. Luc. 1.. Si ergo offers munus incarnationis Christi, quae facta est in ventre virginis, non est acceptum Deo, nisi de simila, id est, scientia vel notitia Dei fiat. De hac re siquidem locutionem ab apostolis et a prophetis suscipimus, Verba apostolorum sunt panes, lagana prophetarum. Quanto enim panes laganis, ad nutriendum aptiores, tantum praecellunt verba apostolorum verbis prophetarum. Utrique autem azymi sine fermento scientiae saecularis. Utraque tamen in oleo fiunt, concorditer enim ab illis de Christi miseratione scriptum est, quia apostoli et prophetae scripserunt, sed apostoli plenius scripserunt, qui completum ostenderunt, quod illi nuntiabant futurum. &lt;Lagana.&gt;Panis latus et tenuis, qui prophetiam et legem significat, quantum enim distat inter soliditatem panis et tenuitatem lagani, tantum inter Evangelium et verba legis et prophetarum: haec tamen oleo lita, quia lex et prophetia charitatem Christi praedixerunt, qua in salutem humani generis venit.

&lt;Si oblatio tua fuerit,&gt;etc. ISICH. in Lev. Oblatio de sartagine, etc., usque ad et ideo ab ejus scientia recessit. &lt;Similae conspersae,&gt;etc. Quia mortuus est et misertus nostri. &lt;Absque fermento,&gt;id est, sine macula.

&lt;Divides eam minutatim:&gt;ut sermonem passionum ejus, qui per partes processerunt, dividamus, alapas, scilicet colaphos, sputa et vulnera diligenter distinguamus. &lt;Et fundes super,&gt;etc., ut quemadmodum misericorditer pro nobis mortuus est, nos quoque pro fratribus usque ad mortem misereamur. &lt;De sartagine.&gt;Sicut enim sartago media inter ignem et cibum, sic quodammodo crux inter impassibilem divinitatem et humanitatem, quae igne passionis est assata. Et sicut in sartagine mollia durescunt, dura mollescunt, sic in passione crucis lapidea corda mollita, mollia et fluxa solidata. De sartagine ergo sacrificium offerre est de mysterio crucis cum veneratione disputare.

&lt;Sin autem de,&gt;etc. ISICH. in Lev. Sicut in sartagine crucem, etc., usque ad ex misericordia quippe mortem sustinuit, et resurrectionem dispensavit. &lt;Sin autem,&gt;etc. Moraliter, similam offert qui in aliquibus communis vitae usibus bene conversari studet. Haec oleo conspergenda est, quia omnis anima oleo eget misericordiae, nec vitam praesentem evadere potest, nisi misericordia coelestis affuerit. Clibanus autem pondus tentationis exprimit, sartago constantiam et robur animi, craticula multiplicem impugnationem.

&lt;Omnis oblatio.&gt;ORIG. homil. 2 in Lev. Dicat aliquis, etc., usque ad hoc modo verius et perfectius secundum Evangelium sacrificia offers, quae jam secundum legem non potest offerre Israel. &lt;Fermenti ac mellis.&gt;Nihil voluptuosum, nihil suave placet Deo, sed quod habet aliquid mordacitatis et severitatis. Unde pascha cum amaritudinibus manducatur. &lt;Ac mellis.&gt;Gentilis eloquentiae, quae voce suavis est, non re. Unde: &lt;Favus distillans labia meretricis&gt;Prov. 5.. Quod autem dicitur in Canticis: &lt;Mel et lac sub lingua tua&gt;Cant. 4., praesentibus non contradicit. Sub lingua enim dicitur, non in lingua, ut ostendatur paganorum sapientia, et Judaeorum littera linguae Ecclesiae, id est doctrinae subjecta esse. Horum non vult integram doctrinam offerre. Unde ait: &lt;Non adolebitur in sacrificium,&gt;id est, holocaustum: &lt;primitias tantum eorum offeretis.&gt;Primitias enim illius sapientiae offerimus, non totam, sicut Paulus ad Athenienses, inquit: &lt;Sicut vester poeta dixit: hujus et genus sumus.&gt;Quod enim invenit congruum scientiae Dei, non respuit: non tamen ultra testimonia multiplicavit, quia placuit Deo per stultitiam praedicationis salvos facere credentes; unde Moyses ait: &lt;Super altare vero non imponentur,&gt;et cum liceret dici non ponentur, dicit: &lt;Non imponentur in odorem suavitatis:&gt;significans, quia si tentaverimus de exterioribus divinitatis adipisci notitiam, tale sacrificium ad altare non ascendit, sed deprimitur in terrenis, quia de terra est. BEDA. in Lev., tom. 2.. Quod mel in Dei sacrificium non offerretur, etc., usque ad imperfecta quaeque omittimus.

&lt;Sale condies nec auferes sal foederis.&gt;Apostolica sapientia. Unde: &lt;Vos estis sal terrae,&gt;etc. Matth. 5.. Sicut omnis cibus sale conditur, ita apostolica doctrina sermo praedicationis. Ideo praecipitur sal in omni sacrificio offerri, ut secundum Apostolicam doctrinam et institutionem et imitationem operis vivamus. Unde Paulus, ait: &lt;Imitatores mei estote, sicut et ego Christi&gt;I Cor. 4.. Et alibi: &lt;Superaedificati super fundamentum apostolorum et prophetarum&gt;Eph. 2.. Unde et legislator non dixit simpliciter sal: sed, &lt;sal foederis Dei tui.&gt;Sicut enim foedus rationale, sic etiam sal rationale. Testamenti ergo Evangelici et salis Apostolici nos commonere voluit. Oleum in sacrificium offertur, si cum hilaritate offeramus, non ex tristitia aut ex necessitate. Hilarem enim datorem diligit Deus II Cor. 9.. Sal qui stypticam vim habet, et contrarius est melli, jubetur addi sacrificiis: sal symbolum est prudentiae, quae restringit et exsiccat voluptatem. &lt;In omni oblatione,&gt;etc. Placere enim Deo non poterit quod non ad normam voluntatis ejus correctum fuerit. Nam si in rebus humanis tanta cautela agendum admonuit quidam de mundi hujus sapientibus, ut diceret: Omnis actio temeritate et negligentia vacare debet: quid de Dei rebus aestimandum est? &lt;Si autem obtuleris,&gt;etc. ORIG., lib. I in Levit. Secundo in loco primitiarum, etc., usque ad quia littera separabatur a spiritu. ISICH. &lt;Confringes in morem,&gt;etc. Non modo praecepit eos Dei notitiam, etc., usque ad per eleemosynam quippe et orationem scientia divina nobis perficitur.

&lt;Quod si hostia,&gt;etc. ORIG. homil. 3 in Levit. Transmissis caeteris, de salutaribus sacrificiis dicit, quae de animalibus, id est bobus et capris et ovibus offeruntur, et nihil ultra ad immolandum substituitur: nec aves quidem, quae in offerendis muneribus substitutae sunt superius. Qui enim salutares offert hostias salutis suae conscius est: necesse ergo habet ut magna et perfecta offerat, unde Apostolus: &lt;Perfectorum autem est cibus solidus&gt;Heb. 5.. ISICH. &lt;Quod si hostia,&gt;etc. Sunt secundum leges diversae hominum conversationes, etc., usque ad oportet enim eas digne conversari, ut perveniant ad salutem. &lt;Marem sive feminam,&gt;etc. ISICH. Superius in holocaustum tantum mares offeruntur, etc., usque ad id est infirma opera cum fortioribus.

&lt;Adipem qui,&gt;etc. ID. Oportet intelligibilem adipem offerri, etc., usque ad et per deliberationem massam sanctificemus. &lt;Vitalia.&gt;LXX: Ventrem, id est cor, cujus secundo facit mentionem juxta LXX, quia duplicem habet operationem secundum medicos, quia per unam partem alimentum trahit, quam vocant ventrem superiorem: per alteram purgationem discernit, quam vocant ventrem inferiorem. Renes sunt genitalium seminum ministeria, cum ventre et femoribus communicantes. Primum ergo adipem, qui supra ventrem est, et duos renes, et adipem qui super eos est, id est super femora, quae renibus sunt vicina, jubet offerri: in medio enim femoris et ventris sunt positi.
&lt;Reticulum jecoris:&gt;Id est, epatis, in quo delectatio vel concupiscentia. Unde juxta LXX pinna epatis cum renibus auferetur: jecur enim in renibus vim operationis ministrat.
&lt;Si vero de ovibus fuerit,&gt;etc. ISICH. Quem praecipiat offerre bovem, etc., usque ad in lumbis quoque operatio generationis.

&lt;Et caudam.&gt;LXX: Lumbum sine macula integrum, ne scilicet aliud offeratur Deo, aliud adversario. Sufficit enim huic ad veniam quae virtutis sunt non agere; sin autem mala operatur, veniam non consequitur. Unde: &lt;Estote simplices sicut columbae.&gt;Columbae enim nimiam simplicitatem habent, malitiam nullam. Qui de bobus sacrificium offert, lumbum Deo offerre non eget: quem in bonis operibus constringit et exercet. Qui de capris immolat, non habet lumbum immaculatum quem offerat, quia eum olim peccato maculavit. Qui ergo non fuit in peccatis, immaculatum lumbum offerre potest, non qui peccator fuit. Hac causa in sacrificio pacificorum capras ab agnis distinxit.

&lt;Nec adipem.&gt;Propriam concupiscentiam, id est carnalem habere non debemus: &lt;Quisque enim tentatur a concupiscentia sua abstractus et illectus.&gt;Sanguinem prohibet comedi, ne quemquam interficiamus: sanguinem enim edere, bestiarum, id est crudelium, est. Ideo aut omnino additur: ut et proximis parcamus et nobis. Deo autem debet anima immolari, unde jussit sanguinem fundi circa basim altaris.

&lt;Locutusque&gt;etc. &lt;Anima quae peccaverit,&gt;etc. ORIG., hom. 2 in Levit. Recte animam dicit, etc., usque ad et spiritus dux ad virtutem, si eum sequi velit. ISICH. &lt;Anima cum peccaverit,&gt;etc. Nihil necessarium legislator omisit, etc., usque ad unde, &lt;Qui nescibat peccatum, pro nobis peccatum factus est.&gt;

&lt;Si sacerdos,&gt;etc. ORIG. Observandum est quod in peccato pontificis legislator non addit quod ignorans aut nolens peccaverit: neque enim ignorantia in eum cadere potest, qui ut doceret caeteros provectus est. ID. &lt;Si sacerdos,&gt;etc. Terror simul et misericordia, etc., usque ad qui conscientia infirmitatis mordetur. Id. &lt;Si sacerdos,&gt;etc. Pontifex, sensus pietatis et religionis, etc., usque ad Christi morte reparatur. &lt;Vitulum immaculatum Domino,&gt;etc. ID. Secundo invenimus offerri a pontifice vitulum in holocaustum, etc. usque ad in quo passus est Christus.

&lt;Hauriet quoque de sanguine,&gt;etc. Sanguinem vituli in tabernaculum, id est, in coelum intulit: cum post resurrectionem coelos conscendens, vultui Patris astitit, quasi offerens sanguinem passionis, interpellans pro nobis.

&lt;Septies:&gt;pro dimissione, scilicet peccatorum et sub ministratione spiritalium donorum. Sanguis autem passionem significat, secundum illud: &lt;Mundus ego sum a sanguine justi hujus.&gt;Et alibi: &lt;Sanguis ejus super nos,&gt;etc. De hac aspersione Petrus ait: &lt;In obedientiam et aspersionem sanguinis Christi,&gt;etc. &lt;Velum,&gt;humanitatem Christi. Nam sicut velum erat inter sancta sanctorum et exterius tabernaculum, ita caro Christi est inter nos, qui exterius tabernaculum sumus, et divinitatem, quae per sancta sanctorum significatur. Contra velum ergo testimonii sacerdos sanguinem vituli aspersit, quia Christus carnem suam sanguinem passionis cruentavit. &lt;Contra velum,&gt;etc. Multis nominibus carnem Domini appellat, quia operatio ejus multa. Unde ipse Dominus seipsum, modo sacrificium Luc. 21., modo pastorem, rursus vitem, deinde panem vitae et granum tritici, translatis vocabulis nominavit. Joan. 10, 15, 6, 12. Sic et Moyses carnem ejus velum appellavit. Unde Paulus: &lt;Initiavit nobis viam per velamen, id est carnem suam&gt;Heb. 10.. Velum quoque sanctuarii exhinc appellatur, quia in eo sancti sanctorum caro figuratur.

&lt;Super cornua.&gt;Hoc altare sedem Dei, id est Seraphin significat, unde Esa: &lt;Volavit ad me unus de Seraphin, et in manu ejus calculus, quem forcipe tulit, de altari&gt;Isa. 6.. Thymiama, secundum LXX, compositiones omnium virtutum. Ubi enim decet compositas esse virtutes, nisi in sede Dei? de coelo namque ad nos descendunt. Unde Jacobus ait: &lt;Quae autem desursum sapientia&gt;Jac. 3.. Quatuor autem virtutes, sapientia, justitia, fortitudo, temperantia, quia caeterarum virtutum genera continent, nominantur cornua: has inungit Deus proprio sanguine confortans, scilicet majori et perfectiori virtute, ut possint contra adversarias potestates fortitudinesque praevalere. &lt;Altaris,&gt;etc. Angelicarum virtutum. Si enim homines gratum Deo odorem bonorum operum reddunt, quanto magis sancti angeli in puritate naturae permanentes? Si autem peccatum quod Christi sanguine piaretur, non admiserunt, per sanguinem tamen ejus nobis pacificati sunt, et numerus eorum reparatus. &lt;In basim.&gt;Basis, pars altaris inferior, infirmos homines significat. Sanguine enim Christi non solus numerus angelorum restitutus est, sed et homo redemptus: ideo angelorum quoque redemptio Christus dicitur Col. 1.. &lt;Altaris holocausti.&gt;Corporis Christi. Ipse enim est sacerdos, ipse sacrificium, ipse et altare. Sicut enim multa operatur, ita convenienter multis nominibus appellatur. Unde Paulus: &lt;Habemus altare de quo non habent potestatem edere qui tabernaculo deserviunt&gt;Heb. 13.: hoc est, corpus Christi, de quo non licet edere Judaeis; hoc altare est in introitu tabernaculi, id est coeli, quia per ipsum ingressum habemus in coelum. &lt;Et adipem.&gt;Mystice, delectationes et desideria carnis; quae tamen omnia non sunt in Christum recipienda, sicut gulae, et coitus desiderium. Quae autem habuerat, habuit ex nobis, ut sitim et esuriem, et hujusmodi. Haec autem Patri obtulit, ad cujus transtulit gloriam, et nobis in exemplum protulit, ut ad Deum desideria nostra referamus.

&lt;Duos renunculos et reticulum, quod est super eos juxta ilia.&gt;ISICH. Quae fiunt et in sacrificio pacificorum, vel salutari. Et in duo sacrificium dividit, ut sacrificium Christi liceat omnibus imitari tam his scilicet qui inferioris sunt conversationis, quibus sacrificium pacificorum convenit, quam his qui altiora sequuntur, quibus sufficit si sequentia imitantur.

&lt;Pellem vero et omnes carnes cum capite et pedibus et caetera.&gt;Hoc praecipit ut Christum non dividas, sicut quidam dividunt dicentes: Qui de Maria passus, qui de Deo passus non est; &lt;Nobis autem unus est Deus Jesus Christus per quem omnia&gt;I Cor. 8.. Caro enim in Domino omnis humanitas est, secundum quod dicitur: &lt;Verbum caro factum est&gt;Joan. 1.. Unde ait: &lt;Carnes ejus cum capite et pedibus&gt;vel extremis secundum alios, ut per haec verba, eum qui pro nobis passus est, primum et novissimum esse credamus: ipse enim est ante omnia, et in ipso constant omnia. &lt;Cum intestinis et fimo,&gt;LXX: cum ventre et stercore. Venter autem significat mentem; eum ergo qui pro nobis passus est, mentem humanam habuisse minime dubitemus, quod quidam haereticorum negant. Fimus, peccatum humani generis, signat quod crucifixus in se suscepit. Fimus, cum sit immundus, gerentem non polluit; neque naturae nostrae est, quamvis in nobis sit: sic peccata nostra, quae Dominus portavit, aliena ab illo fuerunt, nec eum polluerunt. &lt;Intestinis et fimo,&gt;etc. ORIG. Forte ad comparationem, etc., usque ad plenius legislator in sequentibus figurat ejus mysterium.
&lt;Quod si omnis turba.&gt;ISICH. Idem praecipit in sacrificio turbae et sacerdotis, etc., usque ad pro ipsis enim crucifixoribus oravit: &lt;Pater, ignosce illis quia nesciunt quid faciunt.&gt;

&lt;Vitulum efferet extra castra&gt;ID. Sufficit nobis conclusio legis ad manifestanda praesentia, nihil enim praecipitur hic mutari pro peccato multitudinis. Manifestum est quod idem peccatum plebis et sacerdotis intelligit, ideo in utroque idem sacrificium ordinavit.

&lt;Si peccaverit princeps et fecerit.&gt;ID. Sicut in spontaneis sacrificiis, etc., usque ad sabbatum enim ad otium malorum datum est. ORIG. Princeps iste potest dici vis rationis, quae intra nos est, quae si peccet, ut aliquid stultum agamus, sententiam illam timeamus: &lt;Vos estis sal terrae. Si vero sal infatuatum fuerit, ad nihilum valet nisi projiciatur foras, et conculcetur ab hominibus.&gt;Matth. 5.

&lt;Hircum de capris.&gt;Non capram, facilem scilicet vel mediocrem, sed difficilem et asperam poenitentiam. Quanto enim quis intellectu praeeminet, tanto, si peccat, pro majori culpa majorem poenam sustinet.

&lt;Ponet manum,&gt;etc., per semetipsum peccatum manifestans, et offerens confessionem suam. Ipse autem juxta LXX, non occidit, sed alii; quia illi est necessarium aliorum auxilium, ut poenitentia suscipiatur, nec sacerdos occidere praecipitur, ait enim: &lt;Cumque immolaverit,&gt;etc., nec addidit, quis immolare debeat, licet enim in sacrificio poenitentiae alterius uti adjutoriis: unde Jac.: &lt;Orate pro invicem, ut salvemini.&gt;&lt;Ubi solet mactari,&gt;etc. Quia similiter placent Deo digna peccatorum poenitentia et fortia justorum opera.

&lt;Cornua altaris,&gt;etc. Super crucem offeruntur primitiae sanguinis qui pro peccato offertur, quia opus crucis et effectus peccatorum nostrorum perfecta remissio est. &lt;Et reliquum fundens.&gt;Omnem scilicet poenitentiam evangelicae praedicationi tribuens cujus intentio est ut se corrigat et salvetur qui poenitet. Unde in principio Evangelii Dominus inquit providenter: &lt;Poenitentiam agite, appropinquat enim regnum coelorum.&gt;Matth. 3.

&lt;Quod si peccaverit,&gt;etc. ORIG. hom. 2. in Levit. Faciens unum ab omnibus mandatis Domini, etc., usque ad cum agnoscit immolare sacrificium laudis. &lt;De populo,&gt;etc. ORIG. Ad distinctionem ejus, etc. usque ad propter nos necessarium ducit. &lt;Si autem de pecoribus.&gt;ISICH. Oblationi caprae quam offerunt qui de populo sunt, etc., usque ad de capra et ove similia praecipit.

&lt;Si peccaverit anima,&gt;etc. AUG. quaest. 1 in Levit. Videtur dicere peccare hominem, etc., usque ad sed statim subjunxit: &lt;Anima quae tetigerit aliquid immundum,&gt;etc. ISICH. &lt;Si peccaverit,&gt;etc. Non repetit quae superius dixit, etc., usque ad quia alterius peccatis vel errori non debemus consentire, sed arguere.

&lt;Anima qui tetigerit.&gt;ISICH. Non corporis, etc., usque ad sed potest dicere cum David: &lt;Anima nostra sicut passer erepta est de laqueo venantium&gt;Psal. 123.. GREG. lib. XXXII Moral., cap. 4 tom. 2. Juramentum proferre est voto nos divinae servitutis alligare, etc., usque ad igni doloris ardemus.

&lt;Anima quae juraverit,&gt;etc. AUG., quaest. 2 in Levit. Quid est quod pro tacito perjurio, vel tacto morticino, vel aliquo immundo nullum sacrificium praecipitur? Pro eo vero quod quisque falsum nesciens jurat, agnam vel capram offerri decernit? an pro omnibus supradictis hoc sacrificium oportet intelligi? Omnibus enim enuntiatis intulit sacrificium expiationis. &lt;Intellexerit delictum.&gt;ISICH. Notandum quod delictum, etc., usque ad sicut sequentia ostendunt.

&lt;Sin autem non potuerit,&gt;etc. ID. Hoc adjiciamus, ut si quid horum princeps peccaverit, hircum offerat de capris, condignam scilicet poenitentiam sibi, qui nec peccare debuit, nec communicare aliis, nec subditos ad peccandum provocare. Quod ergo evenire non debuit, indiscussum reliquit. &lt;Sin autem,&gt;etc. ID. Qui non potest affligere se continue, etc., usque ad quia seipsum plenissime Deo sacrificat.

&lt;Retorquebit caput&gt;GREG., hom. in Ezech. Mors Christi ad conjunctionem sui corporis, etc., usque ad omnes nos sibi verius in ipsam mortem suam conjunxit. GREG. &lt;Retorquebit,&gt;etc. In sacrificio Dei turtur esse debemus, ut caput nostrum ad pennulas retorqueatur, id est, sensus ad virtutes. Per caput, mentem intelligimus, quia sicut caput corpus, ita mens actiones regit. Sed caput collo inhaeret, nec funditus abscinditur, quia mens nostra a carnis delectatione est separanda, non a carnis necessaria cura, nec curam carnis faciamus in desideriis Rom. 13..
